reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine
model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically
complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence
models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on
large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset;
and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that
the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans
of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the
small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Chain and Causal Attention for Efficient Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the theoretical limitations of transformers for entity tracking and proposes an enhanced attention mechanism to handle long-term dependencies more efficiently.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers require at least log2(n+1) layers for entity tracking with n state changes, and proposes ChaCAL, an enhanced attention mechanism that can handle such tasks with a single layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that transformers have a theoretical minimum layer requirement for entity tracking, and proposes ChaCAL, an efficient attention mechanism that achieves state-of-the-art performance on entity tracking with fewer layers, while maintaining competitive performance on language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers require at least log2(n+1) layers to handle entity tracking with n state changes (Theorem 1).
The proposed ChaCAL attention mechanism can solve entity tracking tasks with a single layer, outperforming standard transformers with fewer layers.
On a toy dataset, ChaCAL achieves 100% accuracy with one layer, while standard transformers need 4-5 layers.
On an advanced boxes dataset, ChaCAL achieves 99.1% exact match with two layers, outperforming a 5-layer standard transformer (97.0%).
When fine-tuned on language modeling, ChaCAL achieves similar perplexity to standard attention, showing it can handle general language tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments on language modeling tasks were limited in scope, not assessing generalizability beyond entity tracking.
Evaluation primarily on GPT-2, not extended to other transformer architectures.
Fixed γ=0.9 across all layers, not exploring adaptive strategies.
Focus on entity tracking in natural language, not other domains like code or math.
Computational efficiency and scalability on larger datasets and models not fully investigated.
future_direction: Pre-training from scratch with ChaCAL compared to fine-tuning existing models.
Optimal settings for γ across different layers and tasks, and dynamic adjustment during training.
Extending evaluation to other transformer architectures and domains like code understanding and mathematical reasoning.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the limitations of transformers for entity-tracking tasks in large language models. We identify a theoretical constraint, showing that transformers require at least $\log_2 (n+1)$ layers to handle entity tracking with $n$ state changes. To address this issue, we propose an efficient and frugal enhancement to the standard attention mechanism, enabling it to manage long-term dependencies more efficiently. By considering attention as an adjacency matrix, our model can track entity states with a single layer. Empirical results demonstrate significant improvements in entity tracking datasets while keeping competitive performance on standard natural language modeling. Our modified attention allows us to achieve the same performance with drastically fewer layers. Additionally, our enhanced mechanism reveals structured internal representations of attention. Extensive experiments on both toy and complex datasets validate our approach. Our contributions include theoretical insights, an improved attention mechanism, and empirical validation.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Tracing and Manipulating intermediate values in Neural Math Problem Solvers
papers.research_question: How are intermediate values of latent structured inputs (specifically arithmetic equations) encoded in a Transformer model's internal representations, and are these encoded features used during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that intermediate values in arithmetic problems are encoded in specific directions of a Transformer model's internal representations and that manipulating activations along these directions causally influences model predictions.
papers.conclusion: The case study shows how manipulations in activation space can find a causal connection to intermediate values, indicating that the model has a locality to certain intermediate values, which is useful for enhancing model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Principal component analysis (PCA) reveals directions in the model's activation space that are highly correlated with intermediate values of arithmetic equations.
Manipulating model activations along these correlated directions changes the model's predictions in a way consistent with altering the corresponding intermediate value.
Not all directions with high correlation to an intermediate value are causally influential; some are correlated but do not determine model predictions.
The method combines tracing (correlation analysis) and manipulation (causal intervention) to establish a causal link between specific internal representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: How language models process complex input that requires multiple steps of inference is not well understood. Previous research has shown that information about intermediate values of these inputs can be extracted from the activations of the models, but it is unclear where that information is encoded and whether that information is indeed used during inference. We introduce a method for analyzing how a Transformer model processes these inputs by focusing on simple arithmetic problems and their intermediate values. To trace where information about intermediate values is encoded, we measure the correlation between intermediate values and the activations of the model using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, we perform a causal intervention by manipulating model weights. This intervention shows that the weights identified via tracing are not merely correlated with intermediate values, but causally related to model predictions. Our findings show that the model has a locality to certain intermediate values, and this is useful for enhancing the interpretability of the models.

papers.title: Towards Faithful Natural Language Explanations: A Study Using Activation Patching in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to measure the faithfulness of natural language explanations generated by large language models, using causal mediation techniques like activation patching.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal Faithfulness, a metric that uses activation patching to measure the faithfulness of natural language explanations by comparing causal attributions between explanations and answers, showing that aligned models produce more faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Causal Faithfulness is a promising step towards achieving true faithfulness in natural language explanations by leveraging activation patching to avoid out-of-distribution issues and provide deeper insights into model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Instruct-tuned models tend to produce more faithful explanations compared to pre-trained models.
Causal Faithfulness is a more theoretically sound framework for measuring faithfulness compared to existing surface-level methods like CC-SHAP and Counterfactual Faithfulness.
There is a positive correlation between the plausibility of explanations and their faithfulness as measured by CaF.
Activation patching reveals that models attribute higher causal importance to corrupted tokens and consider alternative answer choices during reasoning.
Patching across multiple layers does not significantly change faithfulness scores, but aggregating effects at token or layer levels shows variations.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational requirements due to the need for T · L forward passes for activation patching.
Token replacement requires edited tokens to be of equal length to the original tokens, which is complicated by varying tokenization schemes.
Activation patching primarily provides insights starting from the corrupted spans onward, limiting the scope of information revealed.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability approaches to develop a more robust and reliable framework for assessing faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of generating persuasive Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) to justify their answers. However, the faithfulness of these explanations should not be readily trusted at face value. Recent studies have proposed various methods to measure the faithfulness of NLEs, typically by inserting perturbations at the explanation or feature level. We argue that these approaches are neither comprehensive nor correctly designed according to the established definition of faithfulness. Moreover, we highlight the risks of grounding faithfulness findings on out-of-distribution samples. In this work, we leverage a causal mediation technique called activation patching, to measure the faithfulness of an explanation towards supporting the explained answer. Our proposed metric, Causal Faithfulness quantifies the consistency of causal attributions between explanations and the corresponding model outputs as the indicator of faithfulness. We experimented across models varying from 2B to 27B parameters and found that models that underwent alignment tuning tend to produce more faithful and plausible explanations. We find that Causal Faithfulness is a promising improvement over existing faithfulness tests by taking into account the model's internal computations and avoiding out of distribution concerns that could otherwise undermine the validity of faithfulness assessments. We release the code in \url{https://github.com/wj210/Causal-Faithfulness}

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict Language Model Out-of-Distribution Behaviors
papers.research_question: Can internal causal mechanisms be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples?
papers.core_contribution: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and the paper proposes two methods (counterfactual simulation and value probing) that outperform causal-agnostic approaches.
papers.conclusion: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and causal analysis of language models is not only explanatory but also predictive, contributing to reliability and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Internal causal mechanisms can be used to predict model out-of-distribution behaviors.
Counterfactual simulation and value probing achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings.
Causal features are more robust than non-causal ones under distribution shifts.
papers.limitation:
The linearity assumption embedded in the chosen localization method may not hold for non-linear representations.
Reliance on prior knowledge to propose high-level causal models.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research now offers a variety of techniques for identifying abstract internal mechanisms in neural networks. Can such techniques be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples? In this work, we provide a positive answer to this question. Through a diverse set of language modeling tasks--including symbol manipulation, knowledge retrieval, and instruction following--we show that the most robust features for correctness prediction are those that play a distinctive causal role in the model's behavior. Specifically, we propose two methods that leverage causal mechanisms to predict the correctness of model outputs: counterfactual simulation (checking whether key causal variables are realized) and value probing (using the values of those variables to make predictions). Both achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform methods that rely on causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings, where predicting model behaviors is more crucial. Our work thus highlights a novel and significant application for internal causal analysis of language models.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Visualizing Attention in Transformer-Based Language Representation Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents an open-source visualization tool for multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language models, extending prior work with three granularity levels (attention-head, model, and neuron views) and demonstrating its use on BERT and GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a tool for visualizing attention in Transformer-based language models, demonstrates its application on BERT and GPT-2, and outlines future work including empirical evaluation and interface integration.
papers.key_findings:
The tool can visualize attention patterns at three levels, revealing positional and lexical patterns in attention heads.
The attention-head view can be used to detect potential model bias, such as gender bias in coreference resolution in GPT-2.
The model view can identify recurring patterns, such as null attention to the first token, suggesting a potential design improvement.
The neuron view can link specific neurons in the query and key vectors to model behavior, such as a distance-decaying attention pattern.
The tool provides actionable insights for model interpretation and potential intervention, such as manipulating neurons to control attention behavior.
future_direction: Empirically evaluate how attention impacts model predictions across a range of tasks.
Integrate the three views (attention-head, model, neuron) into a unified interface.
Visualize the value vectors in addition to the queries and keys, and enable users to manipulate the model by modifying attention or editing individual neurons.
papers.abstract: We present an open-source tool for visualizing multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language representation models. The tool extends earlier work by visualizing attention at three levels of granularity: the attention-head level, the model level, and the neuron level. We describe how each of these views can help to interpret the model, and we demonstrate the tool on the BERT model and the OpenAI GPT-2 model. We also present three use cases for analyzing GPT-2: detecting model bias, identifying recurring patterns, and linking neurons to model behavior.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Feeling the Strength but Not the Source: Partial Introspection in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can large language models introspect, that is, accurately detect perturbations to their own internal states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that apparent introspective success in binary detection tasks is explained by global logit shifts, but models exhibit partial introspection on differential tasks (localization and strength comparison) only for early-layer injections, with a mechanistic account based on attention routing and residual stream recovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds evidence for partial introspection in LLMs, but only for early-layer injections and on tasks requiring differential sensitivity, cautioning against treating self-reports as reliable safety signals and suggesting introspection relies on general-purpose computational mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Binary detection accuracy is fully explained by intervention-induced global logit shifts that bias models toward affirmative responses, not genuine introspection.
Models can localize which of ten sentences received an injection (up to 88% accuracy) and discriminate relative injection strengths (up to 83% accuracy) far above chance, but only for injections in early layers (L0-L5).
Introspection capabilities are layer-dependent: performance collapses to chance for injections in later layers (L15+).
Mechanistically, attention heads detect perturbations across all layers, but successful introspection requires sufficient downstream computational depth (layers 4-20) for signal integration before residual recovery dynamics attenuate the perturbation.
The residual stream actively recovers from perturbations over subsequent layers, exponentially attenuating the injection signal, explaining why late-layer injections fail to influence outputs.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single model (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), so generalizability to other models is unknown.
Introspection capabilities are only observed for early-layer injections and not for late layers.
Binary detection tasks are confounded by global logit shifts, which may lead to overestimation of introspection.
future_direction: Evaluate whether these effects scale with model size and architecture (e.g., recurrence/looping that extends the integration window).
Stress-test robustness under adversarial prompts, distribution shift, and multiple simultaneous injections.
Compare native self-report to trained activation-to-language systems and fine-tuned introspection models on bias-resistant localization and strength benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic claims that frontier models can sometimes detect and name injected "concepts" represented as activation directions. We test the robustness of these claims. First, we reproduce Anthropic's multi-turn "emergent introspection" result on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, finding that the model identifies and names the injected concept 20 percent of the time under Anthropic's original pipeline, exactly matching their reported numbers and thus showing that introspection is not exclusive to very large or capable models. Second, we systematically vary the inference prompt and find that introspection is fragile: performance collapses on closely related tasks such as multiple-choice identification of the injected concept or different prompts of binary discrimination of whether a concept was injected at all. Third, we identify a contrasting regime of partial introspection: the same model can reliably classify the strength of the coefficient of a normalized injected concept vector (as weak / moderate / strong / very strong) with up to 70 percent accuracy, far above the 25 percent chance baseline. Together, these results provide more evidence for Anthropic's claim that language models effectively compute a function of their baseline, internal representations during introspection; however, these self-reports about those representations are narrow and prompt-sensitive. Our code is available at https://github.com/elyhahami18/CS2881-Introspection.

papers.title: Probing for Incremental Parse States in Autoregressive Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do autoregressive language models maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures, and do these representations mediate next-word predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive language models learn stack-like representations of incremental syntactic structures that mediate next-word predictions, and these representations can be extracted and intervened upon using probing methods.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive language models learn to maintain and update implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures through pretraining, and these representations can be probed and used to control model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes, indicating that implicit syntactic representations guide next-word predictions.
Probes can causally intervene on model representations to steer model behavior, e.g., making certain syntactic continuations more likely.
The MLP Action Probe (MAP) performs best among the probes, suggesting that stack-based representations are important for incremental parsing in language models.
Autoregressive language models maintain implicit incremental syntactic structures that are dynamically updated during processing.
The geometric probe (GAP) makes strong assumptions about representation geometry and underperforms compared to MAP.
papers.limitation:
The question of what constitutes a probe remains a potential confound.
Counterfactual effects, though significant, are small in absolute terms.
Probes rely on a particular oracle (ArcStandard); other oracles might be better suited.
papers.abstract: Next-word predictions from autoregressive neural language models show remarkable sensitivity to syntax. This work evaluates the extent to which this behavior arises as a result of a learned ability to maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures. We extend work in syntactic probing to the incremental setting and present several probes for extracting incomplete syntactic structure (operationalized through parse states from a stack-based parser) from autoregressive language models. We find that our probes can be used to predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes and causally intervene on model representations and steer model behavior. This suggests implicit incremental syntactic inferences underlie next-word predictions in autoregressive neural language models.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Chess as a Testbed for Language Model State Tracking
papers.research_question: How well can transformer language models track the world state underlying symbolic data, using chess as a testbed?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes chess as a testbed for evaluating world state tracking in language models, introduces RAP to probe state, and shows transformers can learn state tracking with enough data or with RAP for small data.
papers.conclusion: Chess provides a useful testbed for evaluating state tracking in language models, and transformers can learn to track state but benefit from auxiliary information like RAP when data is limited.
papers.key_findings:
With enough training data, transformer language models can learn to track piece locations and predict legal moves with high accuracy.
For small training sets, providing board state information via RAP during training yields significant improvements in state tracking.
Transformer language models require access to the entire game history (full attention); limiting attention results in performance drop.
Transformers are robust to distribution shift introduced by RAP tokens during training.
RAP helps improve piece tracking, especially for small datasets.
future_direction: Introduce world state or linguistic analyzer outputs via RAP-like tokens during pre-training and fine-tuning.
Use the proposed benchmark to guide development of transformer architectures that handle long contexts and learn from small datasets.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have made tremendous strides in natural language understanding tasks. However, the complexity of natural language makes it challenging to ascertain how accurately these models are tracking the world state underlying the text. Motivated by this issue, we consider the task of language modeling for the game of chess. Unlike natural language, chess notations describe a simple, constrained, and deterministic domain. Moreover, we observe that the appropriate choice of chess notation allows for directly probing the world state, without requiring any additional probing-related machinery. We find that: (a) With enough training data, transformer language models can learn to track pieces and predict legal moves with high accuracy when trained solely on move sequences. (b) For small training sets providing access to board state information during training can yield significant improvements. (c) The success of transformer language models is dependent on access to the entire game history i.e. "full attention". Approximating this full attention results in a significant performance drop. We propose this testbed as a benchmark for future work on the development and analysis of transformer language models.

papers.title: How Does BERT Answer Questions? A Layer-Wise Analysis of Transformer Representations
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models, specifically BERT, answer questions? The paper investigates whether Transformers answer questions decompositionally, whether specific layers solve different tasks, how fine-tuning influences the inner state, and whether layer-wise analysis can help understand prediction errors.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's hidden states go through distinct phases (semantic clustering, entity matching, question-fact matching, answer extraction) when answering questions, similar to traditional NLP pipelines. Fine-tuning has minimal impact on semantic abilities, and errors can be detected early in the network.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that hidden states contain interpretable information, revealing phases in BERT's transformations and modularity across layers, which can be used for error analysis and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's hidden states go through four phases: semantic clustering, connecting entities with mentions and attributes, matching questions with supporting facts, and answer extraction.
Fine-tuning has little impact on the model's semantic abilities, as shown by probing tasks.
Prediction errors can be recognized in the vector representations of even early layers.
The positional embedding's effect is maintained even in late layers.
The model's ability to resolve question type is relevant for SQuAD but not for bAbI, and fine-tuning affects this ability accordingly.
future_direction: Development of methods to further process the interpretable information from hidden states.
Investigation of skip connections in Transformer layers for direct information transfer between non-adjacent layers.
Fitting parts of the network to specific tasks in pre-training instead of end-to-end language modeling.
papers.abstract: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) reach state-of-the-art results in a variety of Natural Language Processing tasks. However, understanding of their internal functioning is still insufficient and unsatisfactory. In order to better understand BERT and other Transformer-based models, we present a layer-wise analysis of BERT's hidden states. Unlike previous research, which mainly focuses on explaining Transformer models by their attention weights, we argue that hidden states contain equally valuable information. Specifically, our analysis focuses on models fine-tuned on the task of Question Answering (QA) as an example of a complex downstream task. We inspect how QA models transform token vectors in order to find the correct answer. To this end, we apply a set of general and QA-specific probing tasks that reveal the information stored in each representation layer. Our qualitative analysis of hidden state visualizations provides additional insights into BERT's reasoning process. Our results show that the transformations within BERT go through phases that are related to traditional pipeline tasks. The system can therefore implicitly incorporate task-specific information into its token representations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that fine-tuning has little impact on the models' semantic abilities and that prediction errors can be recognized in the vector representations of even early layers.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs.
