Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: An Adversarial Example for Direct Logit Attribution: Memory Management in GELU-4L
papers.research_question: Does memory management (erasure) occur in transformers, and how does it affect the interpretation of model components via direct logit attribution?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides concrete evidence for memory management (erasure) in a 4-layer transformer and demonstrates that direct logit attribution (DLA) can yield misleading results when erasure is present.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for caution when using DLA, as erasure can lead to misleading results. The authors recommend testing effects across varied prompts and complementing DLA with activation patching.
papers.key_findings:
The output of attention head L0H2 is erased by later attention heads in layer 2.
The erasure behavior is causally dependent on V-composition between the writing and erasing heads.
DLA contributions of the writing head and erasing heads are highly anti-correlated, indicating DLA can overstate the writing head's contribution.
Adversarial examples show high DLA values for the writing head even when its input is patched, indicating the DLA signal is not genuine.
papers.limitation: The study focused on a single model and a specific attention head, so the generalizability of the phenomena to other components and model sizes is unclear.
papers.abstract: Prior work suggests that language models manage the limited bandwidth of the residual stream through a "memory management" mechanism, where certain attention heads and MLP layers clear residual stream directions set by earlier layers. Our study provides concrete evidence for this erasure phenomenon in a 4-layer transformer, identifying heads that consistently remove the output of earlier heads. We further demonstrate that direct logit attribution (DLA), a common technique for interpreting the output of intermediate transformer layers, can show misleading results by not accounting for erasure.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: On the Effect of Uncertainty on Layer-wise Inference Dynamics
papers.research_question: How does uncertainty affect the inference dynamics of models, and does model competence affect the ability to adapt inference dynamics to uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that uncertainty does not significantly affect the inference dynamics of LLMs, as probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are aligned. It also provides preliminary evidence that more competent models may exhibit adaptive inference dynamics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit similar token probability dynamics and tend to commit to final decisions at specific layers largely independent of output uncertainty, but show potential for greater adaptability in inference dynamics as model competence increases.
papers.key_findings:
Probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are strongly aligned across layers, with abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers.
Prediction depth distributions are similar for correct and incorrect answers, indicating the model commits to its output at similar layers regardless of uncertainty.
Weak but consistent positive correlations exist between answer incorrectness and prediction depth across models and datasets.
Positive correlation between task proficiency (measured by Cohen's Kappa) and prediction depth difference suggests adaptive inference dynamics may emerge with greater model competence.
The findings challenge the feasibility of using simplistic methods for uncertainty detection at inference and suggest more nuanced interpretability approaches are needed.
papers.limitation:
The study is exploratory and requires further validation on more models, especially more competent ones.
More rigorous tests are needed, including analyses with varying levels of uncertainty and accounting for hallucination on known knowledge.
future_direction: Further testing on more models to validate the results, especially on more competent models.
More rigorous tests that include analyses using varying levels of uncertainty and accounts for hallucination on known knowledge.
Similar experiments for aleatoric uncertainty for a more thorough investigation.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) internally represent and process their predictions is central to detecting uncertainty and preventing hallucinations. While several studies have shown that models encode uncertainty in their hidden states, it is underexplored how this affects the way they process such hidden states. In this work, we demonstrate that the dynamics of output token probabilities across layers for certain and uncertain outputs are largely aligned, revealing that uncertainty does not seem to affect inference dynamics. Specifically, we use the Tuned Lens, a variant of the Logit Lens, to analyze the layer-wise probability trajectories of final prediction tokens across 11 datasets and 5 models. Using incorrect predictions as those with higher epistemic uncertainty, our results show aligned trajectories for certain and uncertain predictions that both observe abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers. We balance this finding by showing evidence that more competent models may learn to process uncertainty differently. Our findings challenge the feasibility of leveraging simplistic methods for detecting uncertainty at inference. More broadly, our work demonstrates how interpretability methods may be used to investigate the way uncertainty affects inference.

papers.title: Toward Practical Usage of the Attention Mechanism as a Tool for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do regularization techniques affect the faithfulness of attention as a method of interpretability? Can faithfulness be quantified? To what extent are attention explanations correlated with human judgments?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that incorporating tying regularization consistently improves both faithfulness and plausibility of explanations obtained through inspecting attention weights across various datasets and recurrent neural network models.
papers.conclusion: Weight tying regularization performs consistently well and should be incorporated when interpreting classifier decisions via attention weights. However, more rigorous instance-level testing for faithfulness is required for high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
Tying regularization consistently improves faithfulness and plausibility of attention-based explanations across datasets and models.
Masked language modeling as an auxiliary objective produces mixed results and is not consistent.
Regularized models attribute more attention mass to words that humans deem important, such as sentiment words in sentiment analysis tasks.
The proposed metrics (change in Brier score and mutual information) effectively measure lateral information leakage and vertical information blockage, quantifying faithfulness.
Regularization reduces the occurrence of adversarial attention distributions, making attention a more faithful interpretability tool.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is on average across the dataset and does not guarantee every instance is faithfully interpretable; instance-level testing is needed.
Datasets may contain annotation artifacts or spurious correlations, which can affect the plausibility of explanations.
future_direction: More rigorous instance-level testing for faithfulness is required.
Datasets need to be carefully curated to avoid spurious correlations.
papers.abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) has been one of the subfields of artificial intelligence much affected by the recent neural revolution. Architectures such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention-based transformers helped propel the state of the art across various NLP tasks, such as sequence classification, machine translation, and natural language inference. However, if neural models are to be used in high-stakes decision making scenarios, the explainability of their decisions becomes a paramount issue. The attention mechanism has offered some transparency in the workings of otherwise black-box RNN models: attention weights (scalar values assigned input words) invite to be interpreted as the importance of that word, providing a simple method of interpretability. Recent work, however, has questioned the faithfulness of this practice. Subsequent experiments have shown that faithfulness of attention weights may still be achieved by incorporating word-level objectives in the training process of neural networks. In this article, we present a study that extends the techniques for improving faithfulness of attention based on regularization methods that promote retention of word-level information. We perform extensive experiments on a wide array of recurrent neural architectures and analyze to what extent the explanations provided by inspecting attention weights are correlated with the human notion of importance. We find that incorporating tying regularization consistently improves both the faithfulness (−0.14 F1, +0.07 Brier, on average) and plausibility ( $+53.6\%$ attention mass on salient tokens) of explanations obtained through inspecting attention weights across analyzed datasets and models.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Information Storage and Transfer in Multi-modal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multi-modal large language models store and transfer information in factual visual question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MULTIMODAL CAUSALTRACE for causal tracing in MLLMs, the VQA-Constraints dataset, insights on early-layer information storage and visual token transfer in MLLMs, and the MULTEDIT model-editing algorithm.
papers.conclusion: This work deepens understanding of MLLM architectures by introducing multi-modal causal tracing, a constraint-annotated dataset, insights on information storage/transfer, and an effective model-editing method.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs retrieve information from early MLP and self-attention layers (layers 1-4), unlike LLMs which use mid-layers.
A consistent small subset of late visual tokens transfer information from the image to the early causal MLP layers via the first self-attention layer.
Mid-layer self-attention layers (e.g., layers 16-17) transfer information from early causal layers to the final token.
Mid-layer self-attention contributions can predict answer correctness with AUROC 0.63, but model confidence (AUROC 0.76) is better.
Editing early causal MLP layers via MULTEDIT can correct errors and insert long-tailed knowledge effectively.
papers.limitation:
Limited to factual questions on natural images with short-form answers.
Does not map visual tokens to specific concepts in the input image.
Editing method could be used to add false or harmful information.
future_direction: Investigate other question types (e.g., subjective) and image domains (e.g., charts).
Map visual tokens to specific concepts in the image.
Detect misinformation in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms of information storage and transfer in Transformer-based models is important for driving model understanding progress. Recent work has studied these mechanisms for Large Language Models (LLMs), revealing insights on how information is stored in a model's parameters and how information flows to and from these parameters in response to specific prompts. However, these studies have not yet been extended to Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Given their expanding capabilities and real-world use, we start by studying one aspect of these models -- how MLLMs process information in a factual visual question answering task. We use a constraint-based formulation which views a visual question as having a set of visual or textual constraints that the model's generated answer must satisfy to be correct (e.g. What movie directed by the director in this photo has won a Golden Globe?). Under this setting, we contribute i) a method that extends causal information tracing from pure language to the multi-modal setting, and ii) VQA-Constraints, a test-bed of 9.7K visual questions annotated with constraints. We use these tools to study two open-source MLLMs, LLaVa and multi-modal Phi-2. Our key findings show that these MLLMs rely on MLP and self-attention blocks in much earlier layers for information storage, compared to LLMs whose mid-layer MLPs are more important. We also show that a consistent small subset of visual tokens output by the vision encoder are responsible for transferring information from the image to these causal blocks. We validate these mechanisms by introducing MultEdit, a model-editing algorithm that can correct errors and insert new long-tailed information into MLLMs by targeting these causal blocks.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Does Object Binding Naturally Emerge in Large Pretrained Vision Transformers?
papers.research_question: Does object binding naturally emerge in large, pretrained Vision Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that object binding naturally emerges in large pretrained Vision Transformers, encoded as a low-dimensional IsSameObject signal that guides attention and benefits the pretraining objective.
papers.conclusion: The findings challenge the view that Vision Transformers lack object binding and show how symbolic knowledge of 'which parts belong together' emerges naturally in a connectionist system.
papers.key_findings:
IsSameObject (whether two patches belong to the same object) is decodable from patch embeddings with over 90% accuracy using a quadratic similarity probe.
Object binding emerges strongly in DINO, CLIP, and ImageNet-supervised ViTs, but is markedly weaker in MAE, indicating it is an acquired ability dependent on pretraining objective.
The IsSameObject signal is encoded in a low-dimensional subspace on top of object features.
The IsSameObject signal actively guides self-attention in middle layers.
Ablating the IsSameObject signal from model activations degrades downstream segmentation performance and works against the pretraining objective.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Vision Transformers and may not generalize to other architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other architectures beyond ViTs.
Investigating object binding in dynamic scenes and videos.
Combining implicit binding signals with explicit object-centric methods.
papers.abstract: Object binding, the brain's ability to bind the many features that collectively represent an object into a coherent whole, is central to human cognition. It groups low-level perceptual features into high-level object representations, stores those objects efficiently and compositionally in memory, and supports human reasoning about individual object instances. While prior work often imposes object-centric attention (e.g., Slot Attention) explicitly to probe these benefits, it remains unclear whether this ability naturally emerges in pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViTs). Intuitively, they could: recognizing which patches belong to the same object should be useful for downstream prediction and thus guide attention. Motivated by the quadratic nature of self-attention, we hypothesize that ViTs represent whether two patches belong to the same object, a property we term IsSameObject. We decode IsSameObject from patch embeddings across ViT layers using a quadratic similarity probe, which reaches over 90% accuracy. Crucially, this object-binding capability emerges reliably in DINO, CLIP, and ImageNet-supervised ViTs, but is markedly weaker in MAE, suggesting that binding is not a trivial architectural artifact, but an ability acquired through specific pretraining objectives. We further discover that IsSameObject is encoded in a low-dimensional subspace on top of object features, and that this signal actively guides attention. Ablating IsSameObject from model activations degrades downstream performance and works against the learning objective, implying that emergent object binding naturally serves the pretraining objective. Our findings challenge the view that ViTs lack object binding and highlight how symbolic knowledge of "which parts belong together" emerges naturally in a connectionist system.

papers.title: Reducing Bias in Sentiment Analysis Models Through Causal Mediation Analysis and Targeted Counterfactual Training
papers.research_question: How to reduce bias in sentiment analysis models by leveraging causal mediation analysis to identify biased components and applying targeted counterfactual training for de-biasing.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a bias reduction method for sentiment analysis models that uses causal mediation analysis to identify layers causally implicated in gender bias and then applies counterfactual training only to those targeted layers, achieving improved fairness without loss of accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully reduces gender bias in BERT sentiment models by using causal mediation analysis to target specific layers and then applying counterfactual training, resulting in improved fairness without compromising accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Causal mediation analysis can identify specific layers in BERT that contribute to gender bias.
Targeted counterfactual training on those identified layers reduces bias effectively.
The proposed method achieves higher fairness (lower Wasserstein distance) compared to baseline methods like full-model counterfactual training and dropout regularization.
The method maintains sentiment prediction accuracy while improving fairness, avoiding the accuracy-fairness trade-off.
The approach is validated on two sentiment analysis datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and evaluated on the Equity Evaluation Corpus (EEC).
papers.limitation: Limited to two datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and one fairness metric (p-Wasserstein).
future_direction: Apply the method to other biases on sensitive attributes such as ethnic groups, skin colour, and country.
Test the method on a broader range of datasets and with more fairness evaluation techniques.
Quantify the accuracy-fairness trade-off in real-world datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models provide high-accuracy solutions in many natural language processing tasks. In particular, they are used as word embeddings in sentiment analysis models. However, these models pick up on and amplify biases and social stereotypes in the data. Causality theory has recently driven the development of effective algorithms to evaluate and mitigate these biases. Causal mediation was used to detect biases, while counterfactual training was proposed to mitigate bias. In both cases, counterfactual sentences are created by changing an attribute, such as the gender of a noun, for which no change in the model output is expected. Biases are detected and eventually corrected each time the model behaviour differs between the original and the counterfactual sentence. We propose a new method for de-biasing sentiment analysis models that leverages the causal mediation analysis to identify the parts of the model primarily responsible for the bias and apply targeted counterfactual training for model de-biasing. We validated the methodology by fine-tuning the pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model for sentiment prediction. We trained two sentiment analysis models using the Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset and the Amazon Product Reviews, respectively, and we evaluated the fairness and prediction performances using the Equity Evaluation Corpus. We illustrated the causal patterns in the network and showed that our method achieves both high fairness and more accurate sentiment analysis than the state-of-the-art approach. Contrary to state-of-the-art models, we achieved a noticeable improvement in gender fairness without hindering sentiment prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models mechanistically implement in-context learning, specifically the components of task recognition and task learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in task recognition and task learning, providing a unified mechanistic account of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The TSLA framework successfully localizes TR and TL components to specific attention heads, providing a unified mechanistic explanation of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
TR heads and induction heads are highly overlapping and correlated, indicating that induction heads primarily contribute to task recognition.
TR heads attend more to demonstration labels, while TL heads attend more to query tokens.
Ablating TR heads reduces both accuracy and TR ratio, while ablating TL heads reduces accuracy but not TR ratio.
TR heads align hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label.
The identified TR heads are consistent across tasks, while TL heads are more task-specific.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanistic underpinnings of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models by reconciling two dominant perspectives: the component-level analysis of attention heads and the holistic decomposition of ICL into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL). We propose a novel framework based on Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in TR and TL, and demonstrate their distinct yet complementary roles. Through correlation analysis, ablation studies, and input perturbations, we show that the identified TR and TL heads independently and effectively capture the TR and TL components of ICL. Using steering experiments with geometric analysis of hidden states, we reveal that TR heads promote task recognition by aligning hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label to facilitate prediction. We further show how previous findings on ICL mechanisms, including induction heads and task vectors, can be reconciled with our attention-head-level analysis of the TR-TL decomposition. Our framework thus provides a unified and interpretable account of how large language models execute ICL across diverse tasks and settings.

papers.title: How large language models encode theory-of-mind: a study on sparse parameter patterns
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that these parameters are linked to RoPE positional encoding, affecting attention mechanisms and degrading ToM performance when perturbed.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that ToM capabilities in LLMs are governed by sparse, low-rank parameter patterns linked to positional encoding and attention mechanisms, providing insights into how LLMs perform social reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, whose perturbation significantly affects RoPE-based models' ToM capabilities, while random perturbations do not. This degradation is linked to a reduction in contextual localization and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern relates to the positional encoding module in LLM architectures. Perturbing the pattern in LLMs with RoPE disrupts dominant frequency activations, impairing contextual localization. LLMs without RoPE lack this frequency-dependent activation structure and exhibit different sensitivity patterns.
Perturbing ToM-sensitive parameter patterns affects the attention mechanism, thereby influencing language understanding. It alters the angle between q and k_BOS under positional encoding, destabilizing the attention sink and distorting the attention matrix.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on false-belief tasks (unexpected contents and transfer) and does not evaluate the full spectrum of ToM abilities.
future_direction: Leveraging ToM-sensitive parameters for targeted model alignment to ensure AI systems align with human ethical norms while mitigating unintended social biases.
Comparing the identified sparse parameter structures to neural representations of ToM in the human brain for comparative cognitive modeling.
Investigating if targeted attacks could degrade LLM reasoning abilities given that ToM capabilities depend on sparse and structured parameter subsets, for robustness and adversarial testing.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interactions with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLMs’ attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Causal Head Gating: A Framework for Interpreting Roles of Attention Heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models in a causal manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for causal interpretation of attention heads, and shows that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, head roles are low modularity, and instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: CHG is a flexible and scalable method for identifying causally relevant attention heads, revealing the distributed and context-dependent nature of computation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CHG scores yield causal insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analysis.
LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits.
Individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity).
Instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
CHG does not reveal the precise computations performed by individual heads.
Occasional divergence between G+ and G- scores.
Head roles are context-dependent and vary across runs.
future_direction: Build on these tools to develop circuit-level explanations of how models implement complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: We present causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for interpreting the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models. CHG learns soft gates over heads and assigns them a causal taxonomy - facilitating, interfering, or irrelevant - based on their impact on task performance. Unlike prior approaches in mechanistic interpretability, which are hypothesis-driven and require prompt templates or target labels, CHG applies directly to any dataset using standard next-token prediction. We evaluate CHG across multiple large language models (LLMs) in the Llama 3 model family and diverse tasks, including syntax, commonsense, and mathematical reasoning, and show that CHG scores yield causal, not merely correlational, insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analyses. We also introduce contrastive CHG, a variant that isolates sub-circuits for specific task components. Our findings reveal that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, that individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity), and that instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.

papers.title: Scaffolded input promotes atomic organization in the recurrent neural network language model
papers.research_question: How does redundancy in training data affect the atomicity of lexical representations in RNN language models, and can a pre-training method induce more atomic organization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that redundancy in training data causes entanglement in RNN lexical representations, and proposes a pre-training method that induces atomic organization, leading to better performance on semantic categorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is a trade-off between sequence-level and word-level learning dynamics, and that inducing an atomicity bias is a promising step towards unified language acquisition models.
papers.key_findings:
Redundancy in training data impedes atomic organization of lexical representations in RNNs.
Pre-training on low-redundancy input induces atomic organization that is robust to subsequent exposure to redundant input.
Atomic organization can be induced in natural language settings and improves semantic categorization performance.
Atomicity is stable over long training on natural language.
The method improves downstream lexical task performance without harming next-word prediction.
papers.limitation: The lack of atomicity might be a limitation unique to recurrent networks that force sequential order during processing.
future_direction: Quantify and compare atomicity in different language model architectures (e.g., recurrent vs. self-attention based models).
papers.abstract: The recurrent neural network (RNN) language model is a powerful tool for learning arbitrary sequential dependencies in language data. Despite its enormous success in representing lexical sequences, little is known about the quality of the lexical representations that it acquires. In this work, we conjecture that it is straightforward to extract lexical representations (i.e. static word embeddings) from an RNN, but that the amount of semantic information that is encoded is limited when lexical items in the training data provide redundant semantic information. We conceptualize this limitation of the RNN as a failure to learn atomic internal states -states which capture information relevant to single word types without being influenced by redundant information provided by words with which they co-occur. Using a corpus of artificial language, we verify that redundancy in the training data yields non-atomic internal states, and propose a novel method for inducing atomic internal states. We show that 1) our method successfully induces atomic internal organization in controlled experiments, and 2) under more realistic conditions in which the training consists of childdirected language, application of our method improves the performance of lexical representations on a downstream semantic categorization task.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
